It is official: The Department of Labor’s (DOL) Fiduciary Rule is, slowly but surely, taking effect. As of June 9, 2017, all financial professionals who provide guidance on retirement plans are considered fiduciaries and must ensure they act in accordance with their clients’ best interests. The rule will impact the industry as a whole, but perhaps none so much as brokers who previously worked on commission, retirement plan sponsors and investors. 
Who comes out ahead and who comes out behind with this new rule? To determine the so-called winners and losers, we must first look at the major advantages and disadvantages of the DOL’s rule. 
Advantages 
Requiring financial professionals to put their clients’ best interests first is never a bad thing. In 2015, a report by the White House Council of Economic Advisers found that the cost of broker conflicts of interests to investors was $17 billion every year. Advisers hold a position of great influence. They have the potential to impact their clients’ lives on a level with doctors and lawyers. The guidance they provide can make or ruin a person’s retirement, which is why the DOL’s fiduciary rule places particular emphasis on retirement plan rollovers.
